p1rubricitems.title: Initial closed form expression for each digit
p1rubricitems.description: The model derives a useful criterion for each digit ensuring that the digit is sufficiently large eventually.
p1rubricitems.notes_for_grader: Uses the base-2n representation of n^k to find a closed form expression of each digit a_i = floor(n^k / (2n)^i) mod (2n).

p1rubricitems.title: Interchanging the floor and mod
p1rubricitems.description: The model derives a useful criterion for each digit ensuring that the digit is sufficiently large eventually.
p1rubricitems.notes_for_grader: Transforms the digit expression into an easily boundable one by interchanging the floor and modulo operations.

p1rubricitems.title: Bounding the expression
p1rubricitems.description: The model provides an upper bound for the number of possible n for which a digit is small.
p1rubricitems.notes_for_grader: Correctly bounds the aforementioned expression, usually by showing the numerator is divisible by n, so that a_i >= floor(n / 2^i).

p1rubricitems.title: Finishing
p1rubricitems.description: The model combines the finite number of sets to arrive at the conclusion that all digits are large eventually.
p1rubricitems.notes_for_grader: Chooses a provably sufficiently large N. The point is not awarded if it has not proven that n^k has at most k digits.

p1rubricitems.title: Sets up the base-2n expansion of n^k with digit notation
p1rubricitems.description: Writes n^k in base 2n as n^k = \\sum_{i=0}^m a_i (2n)^i (or similar) with digits a_i satisfying 0 \\le a_i < 2n, and explicitly identifies that these a_i are the digits of n^k in base 2n.
p1rubricitems.notes_for_grader: Award this when the script correctly introduces digits a_0, a_1, ..., a_m for the base-2n representation of n^k and states both the expansion and the bound 0 ≤ a_i < 2n. Just saying 'write n^k in base 2n' without naming the digits or the range is too vague; the digits and inequality must be explicit.

p1rubricitems.title: Closed-form floor/mod expression for each digit
p1rubricitems.description: Derives a correct general formula for each digit as a_i = \\left\\lfloor \\dfrac{n^k}{(2n)^i} \\right\\rfloor \\bmod (2n), or equivalently describes the i-th digit as the remainder when \\left\\lfloor \\dfrac{n^k}{(2n)^i} \\right\\rfloor is divided by 2n, for all relevant i.
p1rubricitems.notes_for_grader: Give this if the student has a correct general expression for a_i in terms of floor( n^k / (2n)^i ) and mod 2n (or an equivalent quotient–remainder description) applicable to all digits. Explicitly writing formulas for a_0, a_1, ..., a_m in this pattern is sufficient. If they only write, say, the formula for a_0 and a_1 but clearly indicate the general pattern, that also counts; a vague description like 'digits are remainders after dividing by 2n repeatedly' without connecting to n^k/(2n)^i does not.

p1rubricitems.title: Transforms digit expression to a boundable form (interchanging floor and mod)
p1rubricitems.description: From the floor/mod expression, derives a boundable algebraic form for each digit, such as a_i = \\left\\lfloor \\dfrac{n^k}{(2n)^i} \\right\\rfloor - 2n \\left\\lfloor \\dfrac{n^k}{(2n)^{i+1}} \\right\\rfloor or an equivalent expression (possibly via fractional parts) that eliminates the explicit modulo operation and expresses a_i in terms of quantities growing with n.
p1rubricitems.notes_for_grader: Award this item if the script performs the crucial algebraic transformation that replaces the 'mod 2n' with a difference of floor terms, or an equivalent manipulation using fractional parts like a_i = \\lfloor 2n\\{n^{k-i-1}/2^{i+1}\\} \\rfloor. The expression must be correct and valid for all relevant i. If a key step in the transformation is missing or incorrect (e.g., misusing properties of floor), do not award this.

p1rubricitems.title: Divisibility-based (or equivalent) lower bound for each digit
p1rubricitems.description: Uses the transformed expression and divisibility properties (typically n | n^k) to obtain a quantitative lower bound for each digit a_i in terms of n, such as a_i \\ge \\left\\lfloor \\dfrac{n}{2^i} \\right\\rfloor for 1 \\le i \\le k-1, or any correct bound showing that a_i grows at least linearly with n for fixed i.
p1rubricitems.notes_for_grader: Award if the student obtains a correct inequality of the form a_i ≥ f_i(n) where f_i(n)→∞ as n→∞ (typically f_i(n) ≈ n/2^i), derived using the exact digit formula and legitimate number-theoretic reasoning (e.g., showing some numerator is divisible by n). It is not enough to merely claim 'a_i is about n^{k-i}/2^i' without using the mod/floor structure; the bound must be rigorously justified from the transformed expression. A correct bound for just one generic i, clearly intended to apply to all 1 ≤ i ≤ k−1, can count here.

p1rubricitems.title: Exact evaluation and bound for the last digit a_0
p1rubricitems.description: Shows that the units digit satisfies a_0 = n^k \\bmod (2n) = n, and notes that for n > d this gives a_0 > d.
p1rubricitems.notes_for_grader: Give this when the solution explicitly computes a_0 using modular arithmetic or the repeated-division algorithm and recognises that the least significant digit in base 2n is exactly n. They must also observe that this digit automatically exceeds d once n>d. A computation of a_0 without any remark about its size relative to d still counts as long as a_0 = n is clearly established.

p1rubricitems.title: Per-digit eventual largeness (for fixed i, all large n give a_i > d)
p1rubricitems.description: For each fixed digit index i (typically 1 \\le i \\le k−1), deduces from the lower bound on a_i that there exists some N_i (depending on k, d, and i) such that for all n > N_i, we have a_i > d. This may be stated uniformly for all i or separately per i.
p1rubricitems.notes_for_grader: Award this when they correctly translate inequalities like a_i ≥ \\lfloor n/2^i \\rfloor into a statement that a_i > d for sufficiently large n, for each fixed i. It is acceptable if they only write this argument once for a generic i and state that it applies to all i in the relevant range. Do NOT award if they vaguely assert 'for large n all digits are big' without connecting it logically to a rigorously obtained inequality.

p1rubricitems.title: Uniform control of all digits via a single bound or combined N
p1rubricitems.description: Combines the per-digit bounds to obtain a single condition that simultaneously guarantees a_i > d for all digits (e.g., showing a_i \\ge \\lfloor n/2^{k-1} \\rfloor for all i, or choosing N = \\max_i N_i so that for all n > N all digits are > d).
p1rubricitems.notes_for_grader: Give this when they clearly state a uniform condition such as 'if n > (d+1)2^{k-1}, then for every i we get a_i > d' (with justification), or they define N = max_i N_i and argue that n>N implies each digit exceeds d. The key is that they have correctly unified the separate per-digit bounds into one global condition. Vague references to 'for sufficiently large n' without specifying how it works for all i do not qualify.

p1rubricitems.title: Determines the number of digits: n^k has exactly k digits in base 2n for large n
p1rubricitems.description: Proves an inequality such as (2n)^{k-1} \\le n^k < (2n)^k (or an equivalent pair of bounds) for all sufficiently large n, and correctly concludes that the base-2n representation of n^k then has exactly k digits (i.e., indices i = 0,1,\\dots,k−1).
p1rubricitems.notes_for_grader: Award this if they rigorously show that for n ≥ N_0 (often N_0 = 2^{k-1} suffices) the inequalities (2n)^{k-1} ≤ n^k < (2n)^k hold and explicitly translate this into 'the representation has exactly k digits'. It is important that they show both the lower and upper bounds, so that the exponent range is pinned down. A hand-wavy comment like 'n^k grows like n^k so there are k digits' with no inequality should not receive this item.

p1rubricitems.title: Final choice of N and conclusion of the problem
p1rubricitems.description: Combines the digit-growth bounds and the digit-count argument to choose a single explicit (or clearly existing) N such that for all n>N (often restricted to odd n, or another infinite subset), n^k has k digits in base 2n and every digit exceeds d; then states the desired conclusion about existence of infinitely many such n or 'all sufficiently large n' as required by the problem.
p1rubricitems.notes_for_grader: Award this for a correct global wrap-up: they must (1) choose N that is large enough both to guarantee the correct number of digits (using a previous step) and to ensure a_i>d for all digits (using a previous step), and (2) clearly state that all n>N in some infinite set (e.g., all odd n>N) satisfy the condition, thereby proving the problem. Do NOT award if they simply assert the existence of such N without tying it to their prior inequalities, or if they never explicitly conclude the existence of infinitely many or sufficiently large n as the problem demands. This point may be awarded even if the previous steps on which it relies are correctly stated but not correctly justified.

p1rubricitems.title: Set-up of small-digit sets S_{i,r}
p1rubricitems.description: Introduces, for each digit index i and small digit r \\le d, a set S_{i,r} of integers n for which the i-th digit of n^k in base 2n equals r, and rewrites the condition a_i(n) = r as an explicit equation or inequality in n using the digit formula (e.g., a congruence involving \\left\\lfloor \\dfrac{n^k}{(2n)^i} \\right\\rfloor).
p1rubricitems.notes_for_grader: Award this when the student sets up a 'bad n' set for small digits, such as S_{i,r} = {n : a_i(n) = r}, and rewrites it explicitly in terms of inequalities or congruences derived from the digit expression. This can be seen, for example, as solving n^k = r(2n)^i + (2n)^{i+1}t + ... or an equivalent form for n. They do not yet need to prove finiteness here; it is enough that the condition is correctly translated into a formula relating n, i, and r.

p1rubricitems.title: Finiteness of all bad-n sets and conclusion via finite union
p1rubricitems.description: Shows that for every pair (i,r) with 0 \\le i \\le k−1 and 0 \\le r \\le d, the set S_{i,r} is finite (e.g., by deriving explicit upper bounds on n in terms of k, d, i, r, or a similar argument), and then notes that the union of finitely many finite sets is finite, so only finitely many n have some digit \\le d; thus for all sufficiently large n, all digits are >d.
p1rubricitems.notes_for_grader: Give this when the script completes the 'finiteness of bad n' strategy: they must (1) for a general (i,r) show that n satisfying a_i(n)=r are bounded (or otherwise finite in number), and (2) explicitly argue that since there are only finitely many pairs (i,r), the total set of n with some small digit is finite.

p1rubricitems.title: Trivial correct observations about base representations or small examples
p1rubricitems.description: Includes only very basic correct remarks such as 'digits in base 2n are between 0 and 2n−1', or computes a few explicit examples of n^k in base 2n, without connecting these observations to a general argument about all sufficiently large n.
p1rubricitems.notes_for_grader: This item is meant to document common but essentially worthless content. Do NOT award positive points solely for this. It can be useful when reading scripts which consist mostly of numerical experimentation or generic reminders about base-b representations with no progress towards bounding the digits of n^k.

p1rubricitems.title: Unjustified claim that all digits eventually exceed d
p1rubricitems.description: States, without rigorous justification, that for sufficiently large n all digits in the base-2n representation of n^k exceed d (for example, arguing heuristically from 'a_i \\approx n^{k-i}/2^i' or from the growth of n^k), but does not connect this claim to correct floor/mod or divisibility arguments.
p1rubricitems.notes_for_grader: This captures scripts where the student has the right end-goal intuition but skips the nontrivial step of handling floors and modulo properly. You may award a small amount of partial credit here only if the claim is clearly articulated and at least loosely consistent with the earlier setup (e.g. they have defined the digits), but no substantial new errors are introduced.
